text.p: Northern Ireland Electricity reacted with outrage to a statement by the industry regulator that the group wanted to raise the price of power in the region by rejecting proposals for a tough five-year price review.
Chief executive Patrick Harrand dismissed the statement as "garbage". "I have never heard anything so oustandingly outlandish," he told reporters.
"Where on earth the man got this...from is beyond me. We unreservedly refute the nonsense of it," he added.
Northern Ireland Electricity (NIE) emphasised that it was proposing to cut prices by an initial 22 percent followed by a three percent annual price cut in the following four years.
This, the company argues, would cut average domestic customer power bills by 35 stg next year, rising to 50 stg per year by the end of the regulatory period.

However Ofreg, the Belfast-based Office for the regulation of electricity and gas, wants prices across NIE's three main businesses cut by an average one-off 31 percent followed by a two percent cut in annual charges in the following years.
Over the five-year period, domestic customers would be paying 270 stg less than they are currently. Under NIE's proposals, bills would fall by around 211 stg over the period.
Even after two price reviews on the English and Welsh regional electricity companies, customer prices are only going to fall by 130 stg over a five-year period.

NIE argues that the review, which will wipe about 300 million stg from revenues over the period, will allow the company insufficient revenue to cover costs with a "reasonable" return, will materially damage its ability to provide a reliable service and shareholder returns and is flawed.
While some analysts say that NIE could accept the proposals if it slashed 1,000 of its 2,307 staff, Haren said: "We don't believe that is an option for us."

NIE, which has already slashed 34 percent of jobs since privatisation, said jobs cuts would have to be "substantial" -- even if its own less stringent proposals were accepted after an investigation by a monopolies watchdog.
Earlier, the price proposals were referred to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) for investigation. The MMC is expected to make its ruling in around six months.

Bills in Northern Ireland have traditionally been about 20 percent higher than in England and Wales, partly because of the sparse population in the area. It has around half the customers of the smallest English and Welsh regional electricity groups.
NIE also blames escalating oil prices and the high prices indepedent generating companies charge. They account for about 60 percent of customer bills.
However, NIE, which was floated in 1992, made record pretax profits of 107.4 million stg in 1995/96. Gearing is currently only 0.6 percent and dividend cover is a hefty 3.1 times.
